title: The Psychology of People Who Can't Say No

beats.say: It's Thursday night.
You're finally on the couch.
Your phone buzzes.
"Hey!
Any chance you could help me move on Saturday?"
You were going to sleep in.
You were going to do nothing at all.
You type, "Sure!
What time?"
And the second you hit send, a tiny voice says, "Why did I just do that?"
Sound familiar?
You're not lazy, and you're not selfish.
But for you, no doesn't feel like a small word.
It feels like a fight you're starting.
If that's you, you're in good company.
Psychologists have studied why no is so hard to say.
They've asked strangers to write in a library book.
They've tested which refusals actually work.
And they've found out who gets asked the most.
By the end of this video, you'll know why yes slips out, before you can stop it.
And the one small word swap, that makes no much easier.
Let's start with why no feels so dangerous.

elements.text: why no is so hard to *say*

beats.say: For most of human history, being pushed out of the group, was dangerous.
Alone, you were far less likely to survive.
In nineteen ninety-five, psychologists Roy Baumeister and Mark Leary, called this the need to belong.
They argued it's one of our most basic human drives.
So when someone asks you for something, part of your brain hears a different question.
Do you still want to be part of the group?
No can feel like the wrong answer.
Even when the request is just a Saturday.
But here's the thing.
The fear is usually much bigger, than the fallout.
In twenty twenty-three, marketing professors Julian Givi and Colleen Kirk, ran five experiments, with more than two thousand people.
Some imagined being invited to something.
A museum exhibit.
A dinner with a celebrity chef.
Others imagined being the one who sent the invitation.
The people saying no, expected the worst.
They thought their friend would be angry, hurt, and less likely to invite them again.
The people who got the no?
Mostly, they were fine.
Here's the irony.
We all know how little a no bothers us, when we're the one asking.
We just forget it, the moment we're the one saying it.
In one experiment, people first got turned down themselves.
After that, they worried less about saying no to others.
So why does yes keep slipping out anyway?

beats.say: Part of it is speed.
Most yeses aren't decisions.
They're reflexes.
In the late nineteen seventies, psychologist Ellen Langer and her colleagues, ran a sneaky experiment, at a university copy machine.
A stranger walked up to someone about to make copies, and asked to go first.
"Excuse me, I have five pages.
May I use the copy machine?"
About sixty percent let them.
Then the stranger added a reason.
"Because I'm in a rush."
About ninety-four percent said yes.
Now the funny part.
Another version used a reason, that wasn't a reason at all.
"May I use the copy machine, because I have to make copies?"
Of course they had to make copies.
Everyone at the machine had to make copies.
It still got a yes, about ninety-three percent of the time.
The word because, did most of the work.
Your brain heard the shape of a reason, and it said yes on autopilot.
And that autopilot goes further than you'd think.
In twenty fourteen, psychologist Vanessa Bohns and her colleagues, sent students out with an odd request.
They asked strangers to write one word in pen, in a library book.
The word was pickle.
Before they started, the students guessed, that about twenty-eight percent would agree.
In fact, more than sixty-four percent, wrote pickle in the book.
Many of them hesitated.
Some even called it vandalism.
And then they did it anyway.
Because saying no to someone's face is awkward.
And for a lot of us, awkward feels worse than wrong.
So think about the last time you said yes.
Did you decide, or did your mouth decide for you?

beats.say: There's another trap, and it's hiding in your calendar.
In two thousand five, marketing researchers Gal Zauberman and John Lynch, studied how people think about future time.
They asked people how much spare time they'd have today.
And how much they'd have a month from now.
Most people expected to have more free time, in the future.
They were more optimistic about future time, than about future money.
But next month always arrives, just as busy as this one.
So a favor in five weeks, feels free.
It's a problem for future you.
Then future you shows up, and future you, is just you.
Same job.
Same tiredness.
Same Saturday you wanted to yourself.
It's been nicknamed, the "Yes, damn" effect.
You say yes.
Then the day comes, and you say damn.
How many things on your calendar right now, did past you agree to?

beats.say: And here's something even less fair.
The people who say yes the most, get asked the most.
In twenty seventeen, economist Linda Babcock and her colleagues, studied tasks nobody wants.
The ones that need doing, but never get you promoted.
Taking notes.
Planning the office party.
Sitting on one more committee.
In their experiments, women volunteered for these tasks, more than men.
And when they were asked directly, women said yes, about seventy-six percent of the time.
Men said yes, about fifty-one percent of the time.
But it wasn't just about who volunteered.
Both men and women, were more likely to ask a woman.
People asked the person, they expected to say yes.
Think about your own workplace.
Your own family.
Your own group chat.
Who always gets asked, to organize, cover, or fix it?
If it's you, it may not be because you're the best at it.
It may be because everyone knows, you won't say no.
That's the irony of being reliable.
The reward for helping, is more requests.
But it wasn't over yet.

Work that never gets you promoted

beats.say: Because all those yeses add up.
In two thousand five, management researchers Mark Bolino and William Turnley, studied employees who regularly went above and beyond.
Staying late.
Taking on extra work.
Helping without being asked.
Going the extra mile was linked, to more overload, and more job stress.
And more conflict, between work and home.
Of course, helping isn't the problem.
Helping is one of the best things people do.
The problem is the yes, you didn't choose.
Every yes to something you don't want, is a no to something you do.
Your sleep.
Your family.
The project you keep pushing to next month.
So how do you actually say no?
In twenty twelve, marketing professors Vanessa Patrick and Henrik Hagtvedt, tested two tiny phrases.
"I can't," and "I don't."
In one study, people practiced saying one of them.
Then, on their way out, they were offered a thank-you snack.
A chocolate bar, or a granola bar.
About sixty-four percent of the "I don't" group, picked the granola bar.
Only about thirty-nine percent of the "I can't" group did.
"I can't" sounds like a rule someone gave you.
So it invites a negotiation.
"Can't you just this once?"
"I don't" sounds like who you are.
In a second paper, the same researchers found that "I don't" refusals, persuaded other people too.
They signaled conviction.
People don't usually argue, with who you are.
So here's what you can do with all this.

beats.say: Rule one: buy yourself time.
Your first answer doesn't have to be yes or no.
Try, "Let me check, and get back to you."
That one sentence turns a reflex, into a decision.
Rule two: make it tomorrow.
Before you say yes to something next month, ask one question.
Would I say yes, if it were tomorrow?
If the answer is no, the answer is no.
Rule three: say "I don't," not "I can't."
"I don't take on new projects on weekends."
"I don't lend money to friends."
It sounds like a value, not an excuse.
Rule four: keep it short and kind.
You don't need a three-paragraph excuse.
Long excuses invite people, to solve your problem for you.
"Thank you for asking.
I'm going to pass this time."
That's enough.
And rule five: remember the other side.
When you hesitate, picture being the one who asked.
If a friend said no to you, would you stop being their friend?
Probably not.
They won't either.

beats.say: So here's the twist.
People who can't say no, aren't weak.
Very often, they're the kindest people in the room.
They notice what others need.
They hate letting anyone down.
That's a beautiful thing.
But a yes only means something, if a no was possible.
If you say yes to everything, your yes stops being a gift.
It becomes a reflex.
Saying no sometimes, is what makes your yes worth something.
The next time your phone buzzes, take a breath.
Ask yourself if it were tomorrow.
And if the honest answer is no, say it kindly, and let it go.
So here's your challenge for this week.
Say one small no.
Something easy.
Then notice what happens.
Come back and tell me if anyone even minded.
What's the hardest thing you've ever said yes to?
Tell me in the comments.
Which habit should we cover next?
Drop it in the comments.
